hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Can supplements slow cognitive decline? I think a few show promise:

Omega-3s (EPA and DHA) - Important for neuronal membranes, brain function, and resolving inflammation. Higher omega-3 levels are associated with lower dementia risk.

Multivitamins - Daily multivitamins improved cognition in older adults in the COSMOS trials, with benefits equivalent to roughly 2 fewer years of global cognitive aging.

Vitamin D - Supplementation has been associated with a 40% lower dementia risk, while low vitamin D levels are linked to a 50 to 80% higher risk.

Creatine - 20 g/day for 8 weeks increased brain creatine by 11% and improved several cognitive measures in a small Alzheimer's pilot study. This one is promising, but preliminary.

Sulforaphane - Increases glutathione levels in the brain. Early trials also suggest cognitive benefits.

Exogenous ketones - Provide an alternative fuel for the brain, potentially compensating for impaired glucose metabolism in people with cognitive impairment.

None of these is proven to prevent dementia, but they represent promising approaches to supporting brain health through nutrition, energy metabolism, and inflammation regulation.

And remember, supplements should complement (not replace) the fundamentals like exercise, sleep, and metabolic health!

Carrots and sweet potatoes have no vitamin A at all. They have beta-carotene, which your body has to convert, and NIH says it takes 12 mcg of beta-carotene from food to make 1 mcg of vitamin A. Real vitamin A comes from liver, eggs, butter and fish.

Celery is not zero calories. USDA lists 14 calories per 100 grams. About 95% water is true. Zero calories is not.

Apples do not beat coffee for energy. Brewed coffee has caffeine. An apple has none. Coffee wakes you up. An apple is sugar and a little fiber.

Coconut water has been used as a short-term IV fluid in remote emergencies when sterile bags ran out. That is a case report, not a green light to treat a grocery bottle like hospital fluid.

A few walnuts a day have not been shown to boost memory. A 2-year randomized walnut trial in older adults found no overall effect on cognition.

Eat meat, eggs and real food. Cut the sugar and starch. Ask your doctor for a fasting insulin test.

Muscle is the largest consumer of glucose in the body, and it stays responsive to insulin only as long as we use it.

Within a few days of inactivity, even healthy, lean people become measurably insulin resistant. One week of immobility can raise insulin resistance sevenfold, and after a few weeks of it, the insulin resistance can linger for weeks after the person is moving again.

The single-leg cast studies show how local this is. Put one leg in a cast and leave the other free, and within days the immobilized leg becomes about half as insulin sensitive as the active leg. Same person, same blood, same insulin, same meals. The only difference is whether the muscle is working.

Inside the unused muscle, inflammatory signaling ramps up, and the muscle starts making more ceramides, lipids that directly interfere with insulin signaling. The resting muscle effectively creates its own insulin resistance.

This matters most with age. Each injury, illness or hospital stay brings a burst of insulin resistance and lost muscle, and older adults rarely regain all of it. Over the years, those losses stack up, leaving less muscle to handle every meal that follows.

The good news is that the effect works in both directions. Breaking up long periods of sitting every 20 minutes or so, even with brief muscle contractions, blunts the glucose response to a meal.

If one immobilized leg can lose half its insulin sensitivity in days while the other leg stays fine, it's clear that muscle contraction is one of the most important regulators of insulin sensitivity we have.

Midlife isn’t just a dress rehearsal. It’s one of the windows where insulin sensitivity still looks modifiable.

High insulin can cause insulin resistance, and a healthy person can develop it in just a few days.

Insulin resistance is usually described as the starting problem, with high insulin as the body's way of making up for it. That's partly true. When tissues respond poorly to insulin, the pancreas does release more to keep blood glucose in range.

The relationship also runs the other way. When researchers gave healthy young people a steady infusion of insulin for about four days, raising it only to levels the body reaches in everyday life while keeping blood glucose normal, they became measurably insulin resistant. Their bodies cleared less glucose in response to insulin, mainly because less of it was stored as glycogen. Their pancreas also responded less to a rise in blood glucose afterward.

A similar change showed up when insulin was raised a different way. When the researchers infused glucose for three days so the volunteers' own pancreas released more insulin, the amount of glucose their bodies stored in response to insulin also fell, even though their total glucose uptake didn't change.

The researchers concluded that high insulin should be viewed as a cause of insulin resistance that keeps itself going, in addition to being a response to it.

This matters because insulin often runs high for years before blood glucose looks abnormal. If high insulin makes cells less responsive, then a way of eating that keeps insulin elevated from morning to night keeps feeding the problem, even while glucose readings look fine.

If someone is hoping to restore insulin sensitivity, it's clear that bringing insulin down deserves as much attention as bringing glucose down, and that starts with how much and how often a person eats foods that call for a lot of it.

Blood glucose doesn't have to reach the diabetes range to be linked with a higher risk of dementia.

Many people assume their brain is safe as long as they haven't been diagnosed with diabetes. A large group of older adults was followed for several years, with their glucose and A1C tracked across thousands of routine clinic visits. Among those without diabetes, the people whose average glucose ran higher over the previous five years were more likely to develop dementia. The added risk showed up at glucose levels that many clinics would still call normal or only slightly elevated.

The same pattern held in people with diabetes, where higher average glucose went along with even more risk.

This is an observational finding, so it can't prove that glucose itself caused the dementia. Still, it matches what's known about glucose in the body. Glucose that stays elevated binds to proteins and changes how they work, and it drives oxidative stress and inflammation inside cells. The brain is especially exposed, since neurons take up glucose without needing insulin, and the small blood vessels that feed the brain are sensitive to this kind of damage.

The harm from high glucose begins long before a diagnosis. A diagnostic cutoff is a convenient line for clinics, and the tissues of the body respond to glucose all the way up to it.

Because dietary carbohydrate is the main thing that raises blood glucose after a meal, the way a person eats from day to day shapes where their average glucose sits over the years.

If someone is hoping to protect their memory into old age, it makes sense to pay attention to glucose well before it reaches the range that earns a diagnosis.

On the afternoon of 31 March 2017, Pehlu Khan told his wife he wanted to expand their small dairy. He was one of only a handful of dairy farmers in his village of Jaisinghpur in Nuh, Haryana. 
At 55, with eight children, he still rose early to tend the animals whose milk kept the family going. He decided to buy a few more cows at a cattle fair in Jaipur, hoping the extra milk would help during the coming month of Ramadan. 

The next day, 1 April, he set out with two of his sons, Irshad and Arif, and a few others. They bought the cattle, collected the proper purchase papers from the civic authorities showing the animals were for dairy use, and loaded them into a pickup. By evening they were on the Jaipur–Delhi highway, heading home through Behror in Rajasthan’s Alwar district.

Near a crossing outside Behror, motorcycles pulled alongside and flagged them down. What began as a few men quickly became a large crowd—reports put the number near 200. They accused the group of smuggling the cows for slaughter. Irshad later told reporters that his father showed the documents and the receipt of sale. The papers were torn up. The men pulled them from the vehicle.

Pehlu, who had a heart condition, was beaten with sticks and rods while the attack was filmed. His sons were also assaulted. In his statement to police before he died, Pehlu named several of the attackers and said they identified themselves as linked to Hindu nationalist groups. He died two days later, on 3 April, from his injuries. 

Video of the beating circulated widely and the case became a national symbol of cow-vigilante violence. Pehlu’s family said the dairy business collapsed. His eldest son, Irshad, became the main earner, working as a daily-wage labourer. The family sold animals to cover legal costs. They visited his grave every Friday.

In 2019 an Alwar court acquitted the six men who had been tried. The judge cited serious shortcomings and negligence in the police investigation. The men Pehlu had named in his dying declaration had earlier been given a clean chit by investigators. The family said they would appeal. Years later they were still fighting, saying they had lost faith in the process but would continue as long as they could. 

Pehlu Khan was not killed while eating beef. He was a dairy farmer transporting animals he had legally purchased for milk, with papers in hand. The accusation that the cattle were for slaughter was enough. His death, captured on video and followed by a failed prosecution, remains one of the most closely documented cases in the wave of cow-related vigilante attacks that began intensifying around 2015.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.
